titleStmt.title: Response Time Analysis of the Abort-and-Restart Model under Symmetric Multiprocessing

analytic.title: Response Time Analysis of the Abort-and-Restart Model under Symmetric Multiprocessing

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: The Priority-Based Functional Reactive Programming (P-FRP) paradigm, aims to improve the programming of embedded microcontrollers. The combination of purely functional programming and cleanly-abortable event handlers, communicating via transactional memory (TM), makes it possible to write programs as stateless collections of functions, thus making them amenable to proofs and type safety. P-FRP implements executions as function evaluations, therefore, there are no "incomplete" function evaluations, as in the case of a task's interruption. To use P-FRP in the SMP (Symmetric Multiprocessor) environment, we must first understand the response time of programs written in its anticipated multiprocessor extension. Therefore, the contribution of this paper is the response time analysis for the Abort-and-Restart (ANR) event handler semantics of P-FRP for SMP Real-Time systems. ANR is neither a synchronization protocol nor a true scheduling policy. Instead, it is a policy for running tasks where the most important task is scheduled first. Results are derived for both fixed-priority (i.e., Rate Monotonic) and dynamic-priority (i.e., Earliest Deadline First) scheduling. We can say that the Abortand-Restart and the TM models are similar, but also distinct, thus allowing our results to be adaptable for the analysis of TM. 1

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Many real-time programming tasks require concurrency, but correct concurrency is difficult to achieve with many programming languages. Languages such as the Priority-based Functional Reactive Programming (P-FRP) [14] are specifically designed for concurrency and support event-safe implementations making their use the norm rather than the exception. The P-FRP paradigm [14] aims to improve the programming of embedded controllers. P-FRP programs are written as a collection of functions (stateless), grounded in the mathematics of functions and recurrence relations. The P-FRP compiler generates resource-bounded C code, that comprises a group of event handlers, where each event handler is responsible for a single interrupt or event. The semantics of P-FRP require that each event handler executes atomically. Then all of its updates are made permanent. This is based on the event handler succeeding. If the event handler fails, then none of its effects persist. This requirement facilitates reasoning about P-FRP programs and thus is a desirable feature of the language. However, this means that "every" task preemption is an abort action, in other words, a lower-priority task is aborted when a higher priority task arrives. The task is restarted once the higher-priority task completes. Thus by its nature, P-FRP, with its Abort-and-Restart scheme,

div.head: Motivation
div.p: The Abort-and-Restart (ANR) model has an important application in scheduling on multiprocessors and on distributed computing. To date no Response Time Analysis (RTA) for the model SMP and ANR exists. This paper attempts to close this gap.

An important performance aspect of the P-FRP model is that the Abort-and-Restart scheme eliminates the priority-inversion problem, but makes reasoning about the overall system correctness more difficult. We show that in some cases, the number of aborts is limited by the event set attributes or characteristics, so the handlers' response times are bounded. In other cases, the number of aborts is high. The issue is complex and deserves some attention, as it is used in certain design frameworks. For example, Abort-and-Restart is also used by some protocols to prevent packets that do not fit within a specific partition, from being transmitted in that partition. This is typically referred to as idle-time insertion; it is a way to reduce blocking in non-preemptive scheduling. In other cases, the Abort-and-Restart model is used to replace lower priority messages within communication controllers by higher priority ones. This is to reduce the impact of priority inversions.

There is more overhead with the Abort-and-Restart model, since time spent on task execution is wasted. The model, however, does reduce the impact of a wrong decision. For example, it implements executions as function evaluations. Therefore, there are no "incomplete" functions evaluations as in the case of a task's interruption. We argue that the added computational costs are reasonable since the model offers far richer composition than traditional approaches.

div.head: Organization
div.p: In Section 2, we describe the notation and system model used in the paper. In Section 3, we present a review of the existing response time analysis. Section 4 derives the worst-case response time analysis for the Abort-and-Restart model, while Section 5 validates the effectiveness of the proposed approach, through a set of experiments. In the final section, we summarize the key contributions of this paper and provide some perspectives on future work.

div.head: Notations, System Model and Terminology
div.p: For ease of reference, Table 1 below summarizes the notations used throughout this paper. We consider a set of N periodic tasks (i.e., events, event handlers), to be scheduled on M identical processors using a global scheduling algorithm. To avoid potential confusion around end-points, and to prevent impractical schedulability results which rely on the ability to slice time at arbitrary points, we assume discrete scheduling. This means that parameters are taken from the integers and preemptions take place at discrete moments in time. Each event τ i is characterized by a quadruple of non-negative integers (r i , C i , T i , D i ) ∈ Ω, where r i is the arrival time, C i is the worst-case execution time, T i is the period of event τ i , and D i is the relative deadline by which event τ i should be completed.

By comparing Worst-case Response Times (WCRT) of tasks to their deadlines we can determine schedulability, i.e., whether deadlines are met. In this paper, we assume that every task has a deadline that is equal to its period. However, the analysis for the WCRT under RM is applicable without any change to the case of D i < T i .

div.head: The Scheduling Model
div.p: Multiprocessor analysis is very different (and much more difficult) than for a single processor. There are many more possible scheduling schemes -for example, global or static partitioning. With global scheduling, task migration is possible. However, task migration is not free. At times it costs more than task assignment. With partitioning, tasks are mapped to specific processors (typically an NP-hard problem). The partitioning model reduces a multiprocessor scheduling problem to a series of uni-processor ones, by which each processor schedules tasks from the local ready queue. In a real system we are sometimes required to go with partitioning, for example, if there is no support for task migration, or in order to support fault tolerance. In other words, in real systems we may have to use a combination of the two approaches (global and partitioning). Nevertheless, partitioning is problematic if tasks are created and terminated dynamically [22], and often leads to unbalanced load distribution. Moreover, repeatedly calling heavy partitioning algorithms to balance a variable load, may waste computing resources that would better serve the functional requirements of the target application.

In contrast to partitioning, all ready tasks are stored in a single global ready queue, under global scheduling, from which tasks are extracted and scheduled on the available processors. In this way the load is intrinsically balanced, since no processor is idled as long as there is a ready task in the global queue. It is permitted for a task that has previously been preempted from one processor, to resume execution at a later point in time on another processor, and at no additional cost. The advantage of the global scheduling scheme is its simplicity in implementation. It handles dynamic and high load variations more effectively. Indeed, based on results from queuing theory, centralized scheduling models yield lower average response times than those having a queue for every processor [6]. In fact, with global scheduling, the scheduler operates in a work-conserving mode -no processor is left idle when there are jobs in the global ready queue. Global Earliest Deadline First (EDF) is a work conserving algorithm [9]. This fact is the basis for the utilization bound for global EDF scheduling [17]. More information on the advantages of global scheduling can be found in [1] where Anderson and Jonsson show that the average number of preemptions in partitioned systems is higher.

In this paper the global scheduling scheme is assumed. The centralized scheduler maintains a queue of all events in the system. Events are inserted into a global priority-ordered ready queue following the EDF or the Rate Monotonic (RM) scheduling algorithm [17]. At scheduling instants, the processor is allocated to the highest priority event in the ready queue. Whenever an event is released with a priority higher than one of the currently executing events, the event having the lowest priority is preempted (thus, aborted) and re-inserted in the ready queue. Accordingly, this guarantees that the M highestpriority events in the ready queue are selected for execution on the M processors.

div.head: Related Work
div.p: Rate Monotonic Analysis (RMA) was introduced by Liu and Layland in 1973 [17]. Their work presented a test to see if a real-time system could be guaranteed to meet its deadlines. The test was limited in the range of the systems it could address and it assumed that all tasks in the system were periodic, had deadlines at the end of their periods, and were independent of one another. Further work on scheduling tests lifted many of the earlier restrictions where tasks access shared resources, as in Baker's Stack Resource Policy (SRP) [4] and Sha et al.'s Priority Ceiling Protocol (PCP) [20].

The research into response time analysis began with Joseph and Pandya [13] followed by Audsley et al. [3] and Tindell et al. [24] and Spuri [21]. Audsley et al. introduced an iterative equation for finding the response time of each task.
div.formula: R n+1 i = C i + ∑ (∀ j ∈ hp i ) R n i T j •C j .(1)
div.p: The iterative equation is terminated when either R n-1 i = R n i or when R n i > T i (or if a task has a deadline, D, less than its period: R n i > D i ).

div.head: Related Work on Abort-and-Restart
div.p: The idea of Abort-and-Restart is not new: it has been a fundamental part of database design and synchronization policies for many years. Takada and Sakamura [23] presented a real-time synchronization protocol enabling the ability to abort critical sections. This technique divides a critical section into two segments and assigns a priority ceiling to each. Tasks that have a higher priority than the priority ceiling of the currently executed segment can abort the critical section. When necessary, executed critical sections inherit the priority of the blocked task. However, priority inheritance protocols have notable disadvantages. For example, inheritance algorithms are complicated and easy to get wrong. Many more disadvantages are described in [25]. Vitek et al. [18] present a concurrency-control abstraction for real-time Java called Preemptible Atomic Region (PAR), which is very similar to the transaction mechanism. PAR is a sequence of instructions guaranteed to execute atomically. If a higher-priority task is released, the PAR is rolled back and the higher-priority task executes as if the lower-priority task never ran. Once the lower-priority task is rescheduled, the PAR restarts. Ringenburg et al. [19] present software transactions (STMs) based on atomicity and rollback. An STM prohibits interleaved computation in atomic blocks while ensuring fairness (as defined by Grossman in [10]). An atomic block must run as though no other thread runs in parallel and must eventually commit its computation results. Ringenburg et al. use logging and rollback to abort uncompleted atomic blocks upon thread preemption and retry them when the thread is rescheduled.

div.head: The Response Time Analysis Problem
div.p: For uniprocessor systems, RTA relies on the concepts of the critical instant and busy period. A critical instant of a task is an arrival time of an instance when it suffers the worst possible interference. This allows for finding the worst possible response time for the considered task. For fixed priority scheduling, the simultaneous activation of all tasks represents a critical instant [17]. For EDF, things slightly change in that the worst-case is not necessarily given by an instance arriving when all other tasks are contemporarily released. The notion of a critical instant may still be useful, since it can be proved [5] that the worst-case response time for a task can be found inside a continuously backlogged interval, starting with the synchronous arrival of all tasks. This interval is often called the busy period.

In a fixed-priority system, the feasibility analysis of a task set is indeed carried out by computing the worst-case response times [24]. It can be solved by examining a single critical instant. However, when Abort-and-Restart is used, it requires checking the arrival of every job for the task set, and this would be computationally intractable for non-trivial task sets. Therefore, since we do not have a critical instant with which to check the exact worst-case behavior, an alternative would be to consider an upper bound on the delay-costs a task might experience. For example, we could consider a particular job of event τ i that is subject to the maximum possible delay (i.e., interference, blocking, aborts-and-restarts). Although we do not know the location of this exact job instance, we can still denote it with τ * i , and its release time with r * i , because f * i =R i . Therefore, computing an upper bound on the finishing time of τ * i would give a valid upper bound on the response time of τ i .

div.head: Transactional Memory
div.p: Before presenting the response time analysis for the system just described, we will briefly discuss the problem of how shared data is accessed under the SMP-ANR (Symmetric Multiprocessing and Abort-and-Restart) model. When an event handler is aborted, shared data is already in a stable state under single-processor systems. To use P-FRP in the multi-core environment, the underlying primitives must also be safe, fast and scalable. Instead of achieving thread coordination with traditional lock-based synchronization, transactional memory (TM) [8,11,12,15,16] has been proposed as an alternative way to synchronize threads. SMP-ANR implements TM using optimistic concurrency control, in which an event executes without building up a log of all of the transactional variables that it has read. The model handles optimistic transactions quite naturally -no locking traded for abort or merge at commit time (a common paradigm in version control). Therefore, there is less blocking time but wasted processing time. Shared data is read into scratch variables at the beginning of the event handler's execution. Each event then periodically scans the header timestamp field of the TM. If an update has occurred, then the event aborts-and-restarts.

The SMP-ANR model implements locks using a server. In this approach, a server executes all updates to the TM in place of the requesting event. The server is essentially the lock and the manager of the TM. Events request the server's services when committing an update. During a commit operation, the server verifies the timestamp field of the TM to guarantee that the event has seen a consistent view of the data. If the validation is successful, the server updates the TM. Otherwise, the server sends an abort message to the event. In [2], Holman and Anderson tested a server-based approach for supporting critical sections under Pfair scheduling. They claim that the use of a server model makes blocking-terms computations straightforward and the responsiveness of the server more predictable. Nevertheless, the SMP-ANR server design is even less complex, as it is based on a simple thread and event model.

Transactions have long been used for fault-tolerance in databases and distributed systems. By aborting a transaction (an event), we provide a kill-safe mechanism for avoiding the kind of consistency problems that Flatt and Findler describe [7]. We have already stressed that events are composable. For example, a restoration from the scratch variables at the end of the event handler is performed. The local CPU interrupts are also disabled during the TM update to prevent a higherpriority task from commandeering the processor as the lower-priority event waits for a message from the server (either an abort or success depending on result of the update). Neither logging nor validation is required. If the computation part of an event handler is interrupted, values in the temporary scratch variables are simply discarded. A handler does not affect the program state until restoration. When an event handler is aborted, shared data is already in a stable state and so checkpointing is not required.

The TM implementation guarantees that one event can force another event to abort only when the first one commits. As a result, the TM implementation is lock-free in the sense that it guarantees, at any time, that some running event can successfully commit. We will show that transactional memory offers an alternative, and hopefully a better way to coordinate concurrent events. As an example of how the TM model works with fixed-priority (RM) scheduling, consider the task-set given in Table 2. Starvation is therefore possible. For example, an event that runs for a long time may repeatedly conflict with events having shorter worstcase execution times, higher-priorities, or shorter absolute deadlines when using EDF scheduling. However, allowing restarts reduces the impact of a wrong decision, as there are no incomplete function evaluations as in the case of a preempted task.

div.head: RTA for Fixed-Priority Scheduling (FPS) with Aborts
div.p: Most classical scheduling theories deal with fixed-priority scheduling. Remember that in fixed priority scheduling, tasks are statically assigned fixed priorities. FPS was introduced to bring flexibility to task scheduling. When analyzing the basic principles of Abort-and-Restart with fixed-priority scheduling (FPS), three elements influence the response time: blocking, interference, and Abortand-Restart costs.

When disabled interrupts are used, a task can update the shared data without fear that any other task will preempt it. Therefore, there are only two priorities: preemptible and interrupts disabled. With no third priority, inversion is impossible. However, disabling interrupts, (described in section 4.1), still blocks higher-priority tasks from preempting the lower-priority task. This blocking time represents the longest time a task τ i can be deferred due to the execution of a critical section of a lower-priority task on the same processor. This can be incorporated into our analysis by adding B int i to the computation. We must also include the waiting delay, B s i , while events request the server's assistance when committing an update.

The interference that a higher-priority task τ j produces increases the response time of a lower priority task. The interference I i (a, b) on a task τ i over an interval [a, b] is the cumulative length of all intervals in which task τ i is backlogged but cannot be scheduled on any processor due to the current execution of M higher priority tasks. Thus, for a general task τ i , it is intuitively clear that the interference that a task τ j causes on a task τ i in an interval [a, b), cannot be greater than the workload of task τ j in the same interval. Thus, the maximum interference is computed as follows:

div.p: Thus, for a general task τ i , it is intuitively clear that the interference that a task τ j causes on a task τ i in an interval [a, b), cannot be greater than the workload of task τ j in the same interval.

Aborting a task is the same as applying preemption, but with one major difference: In the case of preemption, task τ i can continue at the place where it was interrupted. In the case of restart, the task τ i must start the processing all over again. The time spent is wasted and recorded as lost time, α i , and is computed where α hp i is the upper bound cost of aborting task τ i under higher-priority interrupts.

div.p: The abort costs equations are simply a sum of the work lost. Each release of a task τ j will cause a max abort cost equal to C i , the worstcase execution time of task τ i . For example, if task τ j is released 6 times while task τ i is trying to execute, then there are 6 units of interference which causes task τ i to abort. If task τ j is not released again, then this will be the end of the busy period unless some other higher-priority task is released.

div.head: Calculating the Maximum Response Time
div.p: The worst-case (upper-bound) response time, WCRT ub i , of task τ i is the maximum time from the release of task τ i to the time that task τ i completes, ( f i -r i ). If s i equals r i and the execution of task τ i is not interrupted, then WCRT ub i is equal to C i . However, when higher-priority tasks are ready, lower-priority tasks that are currently executing are preempted (aborted), and returned to the ready queue. Thus, the upper response time for each task in the system can be calculated using Theorem 1.

div.head: RTA for EDF Scheduling with Abort-and-Restart
div.p: When tasks are scheduled with EDF and Abort-and-Restart, it is necessary to consider more task releases to see which one suffers the maximum interference and aborts from other tasks with shorter deadlines. Although more releases must be considered, it is possible to derive a formula for computing each response time in a manner similar to that given above for FPS. The interference in the interval [r * i , r * i +D i ) is also carried out by a recursive approach. For example, by time f i , f i / T j instances of task τ j are released, for j = i. div.p: When considering shared resources such as (TM), blocking, and aborts, EDF and FPS are similar, but where FPS suffers priority inversion, EDF suffers deadline inversion when an event wants to execute, but is currently blocked by another event with a longer deadline. With FPS, because priorities are static, it is simple to determine which task can delay the task currently being analyzed. With EDF this relationship is dynamic as it depends on which tasks (with longer deadlines) are active when the task is released. Therefore, when an event is released, it can only preempt (abort) the currently executing event if its absolute deadline is shorter. div.p: Schedulability tests are available for the traditional preemptive and non-preemptive models, but not for the Abort-and-Restart model. Nevertheless, RTA does tell us the worst-case response time bound (WCRT) for a task, while a schedulability test tells us whether a task set can meet the specified deadlines under a given scheduler. However, determining this may require knowing the WCRT for each task. A schedulability test can then be performed by repeating the iteration described above for every task τ i ∈ Ω. If every task completes its execution by its deadline, then the task set is schedulable.

div.head: Experimental Results
div.p: To evaluate the performance of the Abort-and-Restart model, we present some experiments using real hardware. The control principles that we implemented and tested are very similar to industrial applications that control a Mars Rover or even a Missile Seeker System. The hardware board used to evaluate the algorithms was designed and built around a standard 32-bit micro-controller running C-compiled We used the Parallax P8X32 Propeller, introduced in 2006 as a multi-core architecture parallel micro-controller with eight 32-bit RISC CPU cores.

The P8X32 Propeller chip has 8 processors (called cogs) which have their own memory. All processors process instructions simultaneously so it is a true multi-processing chip. All processors share a "hub" resource and this sharing is timed evenly between processors. It is a different architecture than that of a multi-core chip like the Intel Core 2 Duo processor, but for all intents and purposes it functions the same way. The main difference is that it is scaled down in all aspects (it uses 32-bit processors rather than 64 or 128 bit ones; it has a smaller memory space for programs and RAM and fewer I/O pins). It also runs at much slower clock rates.

Figure 2 shows the basic schematic. The multi-processor chip loads the code from an external EEPROM on startup. The chip uses an RC circuit to generate timing. However, for better timing performance an external 5MHz crystal was added. The speed is multiplied internally to 80MHz. The chip's RESET pin is pulled high by R1 under normal operation, and button S1 is pressed to bring the signal low and cause a microprocessor reset. The SDA is a bidirectional pin on the EEPROM used to transfer addresses and data into and out of the device. It is an open drain terminal so it requires a pull-up resistor. For normal data transfer, SDA is allowed to change only during SCL (serial clock) low. Changes during SCL high are reserved for indicating the Start and Stop conditions. Finally, the reset pulse circuit was added so that the PC can reset the test board for programming.

There is no inherent interrupt support in the Propeller. The chip was designed with the thought that a processor could be assigned to any particular event that we would normally use an interrupt. Each processor can be individually set to run or stop at any time as directed by the Abort-and-Restart application. Having multiple processors available gives the ability to dedicate processors exclusively to high-priority tasks, so there are no low-priority tasks being handled in the same processor as a high-priority task. If we had 2 high priority tasks, 4 medium priority tasks, and 8 low-priority tasks, we would assign one processor to each high-priority task (2 processors), one processor for every two med-priority tasks (2 more processors), and probably one processor for all the low priority tasks-a total of 5 processors. There are also different methods of multi-tasking. In a simple case, a master loop would manage the various sub-tasks on which we could apply our own priority-handling scheme. We can also use hardware counters to track the occurrence of an event. Each processor has access to two dedicated hardware counters, such that if the processor is handling multiple low-priority events, and one is active, it does not miss the fact that another one occurred before it goes to sleep.

div.head: Hardware Case Study I
div.p: We compared the Abort-and-Restart (ANR) model with the results obtained using traditional preemptive global scheduling with nonpreemptive critical sections (Non-Preemptive Protocol (NPP)). The experiments were done on the Propeller chip with randomly generated task sets. For each experiment, we generated 18000 task sets. We varied the number of processors, the number of tasks, and the total system utilization. Each periodic task was generated in the following way: its worst-case execution time was assigned randomly using both uniform and exponential distribution with a utilization mean σ u = 0.25. Task periods were generated according to a uniform distribution in the interval 500 to 6000 micro seconds and their deadlines were considered equal to their periods. Finally, the number of critical section variables accessed by each task is a random value chosen in the intervals (1,3), (2,4), (2,6) depending on the experiment. The results of some of these tests are shown in this section. Due to space limitations, we only explain the most important elements of the results, which we believe are indicative of the general behavior.

The graphs (Figures 3 and4) show the number of task sets that can be guaranteed to be schedulable. It is easy to see that the NPP policy performs better than the Abort-and-Restart model, mainly because time spent on a task execution is never lost. Although ANR wastes CPU time, lower processor utilization is obtained. When a task is aborted and misses its deadline, the rest of the task set is not executed, thus increasing the number of task sets schedulable. Note that the test for NPP and fixed priority outperforms the corresponding test for EDF. This is because with more processors, lowerpriority tasks experience less interference. Moreover, for fixed priority systems the interference from lower priority tasks can be neglected, which cannot be said of plain EDF. This suggests that for multiprocessor systems it may be better to use fixed priority scheduling instead of EDF. Fixed priority scheduling is the simpler implementation of the two, and most commercial operating systems do not provide direct support for explicit timing constraints and deadlinebased scheduling. In fact, compared with fixed priority scheduling, the implementation of deadline-based scheduling requires extra overhead for managing system queues and for updating the absolute deadlines at each job activation.

When we increase the number of processors, the results of the tests remain similar. Even with M = 8 processors, Abort-and-Restart tests for both EDF and RM scheduling failed to outperform those for NPP. However, it is worth noting that the test for EDF with Abort-and-Restart outperforms the corresponding test for RM. This is because more lower-priority tasks are able to meet their deadlines. From an efficiency point of view, it makes sense to use NPP and to refrain from using Abort-and-Restart. Nevertheless, programming Abortand-Restart is delightfully simple, and easy to reason. Our main contention is that Abort-and-Restart qualitatively raises the level of abstraction offered to programmers. Just as high-level languages free programmers from worrying about register allocation, so Abort-and-Restart frees the programmer from concerns about deadlocks and lock acquisition order.

The easiest way to measure the difference in processor loading is to measure the current draw of the chip. We did not think we would see much difference, unless the outcome of the algorithms had some effect on the peripherals. We believe the processors use the same current regardless of what they are doing. If a particular processor (processor) is not running some instruction, it will usually be waiting in a loop-either way it uses the same power. As far as we know, the only way the power would go down is if it is in sleep mode, or the oscillator frequency is dropped. We conducted many experiments to test the hypothesis, but we found no difference between one algorithm and another. Figure 5 shows the current flowing into the Propeller chip while running the Abort-and-Restart under RM and EDF. The Y-axis is the current used by the propeller chip. The X-axis is time. The timescale is the same for all tests. In all measurements, we pass the current to the propeller through a 1 Ohm resistor (Shunt) and measure the voltage. The voltage is 3.3V, so the power dissipated is (P = 3.3V x I). The max current is ∼20mA, therefore, the max power is ∼66mW. The graph in Figure 6 shows that each processor adds more current. However, the processor uses the same amount of current regardless of which algorithm it is running (provided no external peripherals are used). The only way to use less power is to turn off processors (or go to sleep mode). Thus, the algorithm being processed by the processor does not change the current. There is some noise measured since the voltage is so low. There is noise from the oscillator, and there are also high-frequency current fluctuations that may appear like noise, but these are actual current changes that we are trying to measure. The moving average plots filter out the high-frequency 'noise'. Each point on the graph is the average of the previous 25 samples.

div.head: Conclusions and Future Work
div.p: Much real-time programming tasks require concurrency. Nevertheless, certain programming models make correct concurrency difficult to achieve. Programming languages that are specifically designed for concurrency, (e.g., P-FRP, Concurrent Haskell, and ML) support event-safe implementations. With such languages, concurrency tends to simplify the programming process, rather than complicate it. Many real-time programming events with concurrency may benefit from the Abort-and-Restart (ANR) scheme. We have taken a step in this direction by extending the Abort-and-Restart model to Symmetric Multiprocessor (SMP) systems, thus making it possible to treat programs as functions (stateless) and making them amenable to proofs and type-safety. In this paper, we presented a response time analysis for the Abort-and-Restart model. The timing analysis under Abort-and-Restart conditions is itself important and can stand alone as a subject of inquiry. Abort-and-Restart is used not only in P-FRP, but also in databases (in a slightly different form) and other applications. The effectiveness of the analysis has been extensively shown through exhaustive testing. Combining the Abort-and-Restart scheme with the Least Laxity First scheduling and other well-known heuristics remains as a future endeavor.
